text: This course starts in a pot, not on a screen. A pot, or container, holds the growing material and the roots. The part of the pot where the roots live is called the root zone. Look at the cutaway on the screen. It shows three things sharing that space: solid material, water and air. Every decision you later make in the app changes how much water and air sit in the root zone. So you need a clear picture of it first.
title: Start inside the pot

text: Here is the first question of the course. What do the roots need from the pot? Hold your answer in mind. Most people say water. That is half right. On the next slide you will find the other half. It changes how you think about watering.
title: What do the roots need?

text: Picture a handful of gravel. Each stone is solid, but there are gaps between the stones. The material in a pot works the same way. Growers call the growing material around the roots substrate. Two common substrates are coco, made from shredded coconut husk, and stone wool, made from rock spun into fibres. Look at the cutaway. The solid pieces are the substrate. The gaps between those pieces are called pore spaces.
title: Substrate and its pore spaces

visual.alt: Conceptual pot cutaway: solid substrate, held water, air spaces and roots.

text: Each pore space holds either water or air. Roots need both. They take up water, and they also need oxygen. Oxygen is the gas in air that keeps root cells alive and working. In the picture, some spaces hold water and some hold air. Now imagine filling every space with water. There would be no room left for air, and the roots would run short of oxygen.
title: Spaces hold water or air

visual.alt: Conceptual pot cutaway: solid substrate, held water, air spaces and roots.

text: So more water is not always better. Good substrate does three jobs, and the picture shows all three. It holds some water in its spaces. It lets extra water run out through the holes in the bottom of the pot. Growers call that drainage. And as water drains away, air moves back into some of the spaces. That mix of held water and returning air is what roots need. Next, you will follow water through a pot step by step.
title: Hold water. Drain excess. Allow air.

visual.alt: Conceptual pot cutaway: solid substrate, held water, air spaces and roots.

text: Picture a spare pot of substrate with no plant in it, sitting in a tray. Pour water on top. Follow the water in the picture. It enters the substrate at the top. Some of it stays, held in the pore spaces. The rest runs through and drains out of the bottom into the tray. For example, pour in one litre. If a quarter of a litre runs into the tray, then three quarters of a litre stayed in the pot.
title: Follow the water

visual.alt: Example paths: delivered water can remain, drain, or leave through roots and evaporation.

text: Over the next hours, the water held in the pot goes down. The picture shows three ways it leaves. First, roots take water in and the plant uses it. Growers call this plant uptake. Second, water at the surface turns into vapour and drifts into the air. That is evaporation. Third, some water keeps draining out of the bottom for a while after watering. All three lower the amount of water in the pot.
title: Three ways water leaves

visual.alt: Example paths: delivered water can remain, drain, or leave through roots and evaporation.

text: This matters every time you read a number later. Suppose a pot lost half a litre since the morning. The plant did not necessarily use half a litre. Part may have evaporated, and part may have drained. The picture keeps all three paths side by side for that reason. When water in a pot falls, ask which of the three paths it took before you decide what the plant used.
title: Water loss has three causes

visual.alt: Example paths: delivered water can remain, drain, or leave through roots and evaporation.

text: Here is a real situation. A pot stays very wet all day. The leaves droop and look unhealthy. Many beginners think the plant looks thirsty, so they add more water. Look at the three clues in the picture: a very wet pot, unhealthy leaves, and a question about the cause. Think about what you learned on the last two slides about water filling the pore spaces.
title: Very wet: add more water?

text: You have two choices on the screen. The first is to add more water straight away. The second is to stop and find the cause before you change anything. Pick one now, before the answer appears. Which would you choose?
title: Choose the next action

text: Check first. The picture lists three checks. Look at the crop itself: the leaves, the stems and, where you can, the roots. Check the equipment that delivers water, and make sure it stops when it should. Then look at the reading. A sensor is a device that measures something, such as wetness, and the number it reports is called a reading. Each check takes a few minutes and puts nothing at risk.
title: Check the cause first

text: Why check first? Different problems can look the same. A very wet pot with drooping leaves may mean the roots are short of oxygen, because water fills the spaces. More water would make that worse. Look at the three boxes in the picture. The reading, the equipment checks and what you see at the roots each tell part of the story. Put the three together, then decide.
title: One symptom, several causes

text: Think of steering a car. You make small turns to keep it heading where you want. Crop steering works the same way. You adjust growing conditions to guide how the crop grows. The picture links the two: adjust the conditions, influence the growth. This course steers with one condition, irrigation, which means supplying water to the crop. The app you will learn, called Crop Steering, is software that helps you plan and run that irrigation.
title: Steer growing conditions

text: With irrigation you control three things, shown on the screen. When water arrives. How much arrives each time. And how long you wait before the next delivery. The picture also shows what changes how much water the crop needs: light, temperature and humidity. Humidity is the amount of moisture in the air. For example, on a hot, bright, dry day a plant uses more water than on a cool, dim, damp one.
title: What you control, what changes need

text: Steering has a direction. You can manage water to encourage more leafy growth, or to encourage flowering. Later lessons name these two directions and show how to choose between them. Look at the third label in the picture: keep roots working. Whichever way you steer, the roots must stay healthy, so drying the pot as hard as possible is never the goal. Steering guides growth, and the result still depends on the whole grow.
title: Steering must keep roots working

visual.alt: Local probe region: check the exact quantity, location and age.

text: Now the limit of sensors. A thermometer in your kitchen tells you the kitchen temperature, not the bedroom. A moisture sensor works the same way. The part pushed into the substrate is called a probe, and in this course sensor and probe mean the same device. Look at the region marked around the probe in the picture. That small spot is all it measures. Another pot in the same row can be wetter or drier.
title: Like a thermometer in one room

visual.alt: Local probe region: check the exact quantity, location and age.

text: So you use three kinds of evidence together, shown as three boxes here. Sensor readings give you numbers from one small spot. Equipment checks tell you whether water is really reaching each pot. Crop observations tell you how the plants themselves are doing. When all three agree, you can act with confidence. When they disagree, find out why before you change anything.
title: Use three kinds of evidence

text: You will practise in the demo. The demo is a practice copy of the app. It looks and behaves like the real thing, but it runs no real equipment, so a mistake costs nothing. Later, when you set up a real system, start with one zone. A zone is a group of plants that get their water together, at the same time. Starting with one zone keeps any early mistake small.
title: Practise in the demo

labels: New system: start with one zone

text: Time to check yourself. Look at the cutaway on the screen. Point to the solid substrate. Point to the water in the pore spaces. Point to the air. Then name one thing a single probe cannot tell you. For example, it cannot tell you whether a pot at the far end of the zone is dry.
title: Point to solids, water and air

visual.alt: Conceptual pot cutaway: solid substrate, held water, air spaces and roots.

text: In the next lesson you will put a number on how wet the substrate is. That number is called volumetric water content, or VWC for short. It describes how much of a sample is water. You will work it out with drawn boxes before you ever see it in the app.
title: Next: volumetric water content

labels: The water share of a sample
